full_judgment:
12. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, took us through the relevant portions of the petition and the papers and documents annexed to the petition. He also referred to the various portions of the statements made in the affidavits-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 4 and also the respondent No. 3. He submitted that the Review Panel failed to follow the various provisions of the Public Procurement Regulation 2003 (PPR), notably, regulation Nos. 51, 52 and 53, in disposing of the complaint lodged by the respondent No. 4. Besides, he submitted that the Review Panel did not consider it necessary to give any notice to the petitioner whose tender was the lowest and rightly got the award of the contract in its favour, that the petitioner on coming to know about the proceeding of the complaint, even uninvited, went to the place of hearing and made applications for impleading itself but it was not allowed, as such, the learned Counsel submits, this is a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Besides, he further submitted that the petition of complaint before the Review Panel was not even maintainable since the remedies available a priori before the administrative authorities, were not exhausted and without availing its next forum before the Secretary of the Ministry of Finance, the complaint of the respondent No. 4 before the Review Panel was not maintainable. He further submitted that an earlier application although was filed before the Governor of Bangladesh Bank, who is the head of the Procuring Entity, but such a complaint could not be considered since it was filed beyond the period of limitation as spelt out in regulation 51 of the PPR. He submitted that the petitioner being the lowest bidder and having satisfied all the requirements of the tender (Annexure-A) and bid documents (Annexure-B), the concerned authorities rightly awarded the contract in its favour. But the members of the Review Panel without appreciating the facts, circumstances and the economic reality in its proper perspective, wrongly and illegally directed cancellation of the contract awarded in its favour.  

 14. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 4, started his argument by referring to the letter dated 24-12-2006 of the World Bank (Annexure-17 page 118 to the affidavit in opposition of the respondent No. 4) which considered the petitioner as non-responsive since it could not qualify of its own, without the support of its holding or parent company. He submitted that the bid was made by the petitioner, a legal entity, which must stand on its own, to be in competition with the bid of the respondent No. 4 and again, it should not be allowed to depend on other legal entities, such as, the AIT and the PCB, which might have fulfilled the pre-qualification criteria of the project but since it is the petitioner which is the bidder as envisaged under the tender document and the bid document itself must satisfy all the requirements as spelt out therein. He submitted that it is palpably clear that the petitioner company, on its own, does not fulfil the requirement as regards it turnover and other capabilities and other criterion for the last five years as required. On the objection that the respondent No. 4 filed its petition of complaint before the Review Panel without exhausting the administrative forums provided for in the PPR, he submitted that it filed an objection from the very initial stage starting from 4-4-2006 before the TEC, thereafter filed objections before the Project Director on 9-8-2006 and 13-8-2006 who in his incomplete reply dated 21-8-2006 (Annexure-12, page 75), stated that after considering all issues, the results would be made available to all the bidders but, unfortunately, he submitted, it never came, that being exasperated he filed two applications before the Governor, Bangladesh Bank, the head of the Procuring Entity, on 20-9-2006, but no response was received on either of its applications, as such, since time was running out it was constrained to send a copy of its complaint to the Governor, Bangladesh, through e-mail to the Secretary, Ministry of Finance, on 25-9-2006 but that again remained without any response, as such, the respondent No. 4, without losing any further time was constrained to file a formal petition of complaint on 12-10-2006 before the Review Panel, bringing its complaints which were earlier filed on various dates since 4-4-2006, as such, he strenuously argued that there was no lapse either in terms of limitation or forum on its part, to exhaust the remedies available before the administrative authorities before the respondent No. 4 was constrained to approach the Review Panel under the provisions of the PPR. On the question of the breach of the principles of natural justice in not hearing the petitioner by the Review Panel, he submitted that it is very true that the provision of natural justice is an important phenomenon but since there is no specific provision for impleading all the bidders in the proceeding before the Review Panel, the Review Panel heard the complaints of the respondent No. 4 and also the response of the Bangladesh Bank, the Procuring Entity, the respondent No. 3. It heard the respondent No. 3 at full length in support of the decision for acceptance of the tender of the petitioner, it argued everything legally possible on behalf of the petitioner, as such, although apparently it might appear that there is a breach of the principles of natural justice but in reality the entire case of the petitioner was fully canvassed by the Bangladesh Bank in justification of its decision to accept the tender of the petitioner, so much so, that there cannot be any question of the breach of the principles of natural justice in the present instance in the real sense. He further submitted that the Review Panel has accordingly found that the tender of the petitioner was non responsive, firstly, because the bank guarantee furnished by a foreign bank in Bangladesh Taka currency, was not drawn on a non-judicial stamp of Taka 150, secondly, it was non-responsive because the turnover and other criterion for the last five years for the petitioner-company do not satisfy the requirements as spelt out in the bid document, thirdly, the Bangladesh Bank wrongly and illegally allowed the petitioner company for making the additions and modifications of its tender beyond the ambit of its bid documents and the World Bank procuring guidelines, as such, the petitioner company is a non-responsive one and the Review Panel rightly found so.
